L11:   4. cite8†Search approaches L12: # Ranking and reranking
L13: 
L14: Many search systems are built on multi-stage retrieval pipelines.
L15: 
L16: Earlier stages use cheap, fast algorithms to find a broad set of possible matches.
L17: Later stages use more powerful models, often machine learning-based, to reorder the documents. This step is called re-ranking. Because the resource-intensive model is only applied to the smaller set of pre-filtered results, this approach returns more relevant results while still optimizing for search performance and computational costs.
L18: 
L19: Elasticsearch supports various ranking and re-ranking techniques to optimize search relevance and performance.
L20: ## cite9†Two-stage retrieval pipelines L21: 
L22: ### cite10†Initial retrieval L23: 
L24: #### cite11†Full-text search: BM25 scoring L25: 
L26: Elasticsearch ranks documents based on term frequency and inverse document frequency, adjusted for document length. cite12†BM25†en.wikipedia.org is the default statistical scoring algorithm in Elasticsearch.
L27: #### cite13†Vector search: similarity scoring L28: Vector search involves transforming data into dense or sparse vector embeddings to capture semantic meanings, and computing similarity scores for query vectors. Store vectors using `semantic_text` fields for automatic inference and vectorization or `dense_vector` and `sparse_vector` fields when you need more control over the underlying embedding model. Query vector fields with `semantic`, `knn` or `sparse_vector` queries to compute similarity scores. Refer to cite14†semantic search for more information.
L29: #### cite15†Hybrid techniques L30: 
L31: Hybrid search techniques combine results from full-text and vector search pipelines. Elasticsearch enables combining lexical matching (BM25) and vector search scores using the cite16†Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) algorithm.
L32: ### cite17†Re-ranking L33: 
L34: When using the following advanced re-ranking pipelines, first-stage retrieval mechanisms effectively generate a set of candidates. These candidates are funneled into the re-ranker to perform more computationally expensive re-ranking tasks.
L35: #### cite18†Semantic re-ranking L36: 
L37: cite19†Semantic re-ranking uses machine learning models to reorder search results based on their semantic similarity to a query. Models can be hosted directly in your Elasticsearch cluster, or you can use cite20†inference endpoints to call models provided by third-party services. Semantic re-ranking enables out-of-the-box semantic search capabilities on existing full-text search indices.
L38: 
L39: Elasticsearch supports semantic re-ranking through two interfaces:
L40:   * The cite19†`text_similarity_reranker` retriever for composable retrieval pipelines through the `_search` API
L41:   * The cite19†ES|QL `RERANK` command for piped search queries through the `_query` API
L42: #### cite21†Learning to Rank (LTR) L43: 
L44: cite22†Learning To Rank is for advanced users. Learning To Rank involves training a machine learning model to build a ranking function for your search experience that updates over time. LTR is best suited for when you have ample training data and need highly customized relevance tuning.
